planting.note: Plant container-grown transplants or rooted cuttings in spring in lean, gravelly, well-drained soil in full sun to light shade; this low woody subshrub resents heavy, wet soils.

directions: Native to rocky forest openings and roadcuts in the Cascade Range and Olympic Mountains of Washington and Oregon, Cardwell's penstemon forms a low, spreading, woody-based mound of glossy evergreen leaves. In late spring it produces a dense flush of deep magenta-purple tubular flowers that nearly hide the foliage, drawing in bumblebees. Plant in gritty, sharply drained soil on a slope or rock garden where excess moisture drains away from the crown, and avoid rich garden soil or heavy summer watering. A light shearing after bloom keeps the mound tidy and encourages denser growth the following year.

planting.note: Sow outdoors in fall or cold stratify 60-90 days before spring sowing in moist, well-drained soil in full sun; this subalpine species needs winter chilling to germinate reliably.

directions: Unusual among beardtongues for its pale, soft yellow flowers, this species grows in dense, congested whorls along short, erect stems and is native to subalpine meadows and open dry woods from the Cascades east through the Rocky Mountains. It prefers moist-but-drained soil through the growing season rather than the bone-dry conditions many Penstemon species favor, reflecting its mountain meadow origins. Grow in full sun with consistent moisture during establishment, then reduce watering as plants mature. Its soft coloring makes it a useful accent among the more common blue and purple penstemons in a native rock or meadow garden.

planting.note: Direct sow in fall or cold stratify before spring sowing in lean, rocky or sandy soil in full sun; this tough high-desert species is adapted to shallow volcanic or stony ground.

directions: Hot-rock penstemon takes its common name from the sun-baked, rocky volcanic scablands and dry slopes of the Great Basin and inland Pacific Northwest where it grows. Clusters of creamy white to pale yellow tubular flowers, sometimes lined with fine purple veining, rise on branched stems above toothed, somewhat leathery leaves from late spring into summer. It thrives in thin, stony, mineral soil with excellent drainage and little supplemental water once rooted in, making it a good choice for a hot, exposed scree bed or dryland rock garden. Avoid fertile garden soil or regular irrigation, which shorten its lifespan.

planting.note: Plant container-grown transplants in spring in lean, rocky, well-drained soil in full sun; this cliff-dwelling species is ideal for a rock wall crevice or slope where it can trail.

directions: Distinguished by its deeply cut, toothed or lobed gray-green leaves, Richardson's penstemon is native to basalt cliffs and rocky outcrops of the Columbia River Gorge and surrounding dry inland Pacific Northwest. Loose spikes of fringed, bright pink to rose-lavender tubular flowers appear through summer on sprawling, semi-woody stems that naturally cascade over rock. It is well suited to a dry stone wall, raised bed edge, or steep slope with sharp drainage, and tolerates heat and reflected sun from pavement or rock. Cut back old flowering stems in late winter to refresh the clump.

planting.note: Direct sow in fall or cold stratify before spring sowing in lean, well-drained soil in full sun; established plants tolerate dry rocky slopes with minimal care.

directions: One of the showier wild beardtongues of the inland Pacific Northwest, Venus penstemon bears large, deep violet-purple flowers in loose, branched spikes above narrow, dark green leaves, blooming through early summer on dry rocky slopes and open pine forests of Idaho, Oregon, and Washington. It is a reliable, long-lived perennial in lean, well-drained garden soil and tolerates considerable summer drought once established. Full sun and sharp drainage keep it compact and floriferous, while rich or consistently moist soil leads to floppy growth and shorter life.

planting.note: Direct sow in fall or cold stratify before spring sowing in lean, sandy or rocky, very well-drained soil in full sun; a true high-desert native that fails in heavy or moist soils.

directions: Royal penstemon produces some of the most intensely saturated sky-blue to deep cobalt flowers of any Great Basin wildflower, carried in loose spikes above narrow, blue-green leaves from late spring into early summer. Native to sagebrush steppe and dry rocky slopes across the Intermountain West, it is extremely drought tolerant once established and performs best in lean, fast-draining, sandy or gravelly soil in full sun. Avoid fertile garden soil, mulch, or regular irrigation, all of which encourage rot in this high-desert specialist. It is an excellent nectar source for native bees in arid native plant gardens.

planting.note: Direct sow in fall or cold stratify before spring sowing in lean, well-drained soil in full sun; benefits from a winter chill period to break seed dormancy.

directions: True to its common name, wandbloom penstemon sends up slender, wand-like spikes densely set with small, tubular, lavender-blue flowers through early summer, native to montane meadows, open pine forests, and dry slopes of the southern Rocky Mountains from Colorado and Utah south into New Mexico and Arizona. Its narrow, upright habit takes up little space, making it a good filler among bolder perennials in a dry native border. Grow in lean to average, well-drained soil in full sun; established clumps tolerate drought well but also accept occasional summer water better than some of its drier-adapted relatives.

planting.note: Direct sow in fall or cold stratify before spring sowing in lean, rocky or sandy, well-drained soil in full sun; a durable species of pinyon-juniper and high-plains country.

directions: James' beardtongue is a compact, drought-hardy perennial of the Four Corners region, found on dry mesas, high plains, and pinyon-juniper woodlands from Colorado and Utah south through New Mexico and Arizona. Short spikes of pale lavender-pink, inflated tubular flowers appear in late spring above narrow gray-green leaves. It thrives in lean, rocky or sandy soil with sharp drainage and asks for almost no supplemental water once established, making it well suited to a high-desert or xeriscape rock garden. Avoid rich soil or overwatering, which shorten its naturally long life in the wild.

planting.note: Direct sow in fall or cold stratify 30-60 days before spring sowing in lean, sandy, well-drained soil in full sun; a true sand prairie specialist that dislikes heavy clay.

directions: Broadbeard penstemon grows wild across the sandy prairies and plains of the central and northern Great Plains, from Montana and Wyoming south to Texas, where its narrow, waxy blue-gray leaves and clear sky-blue flowers stand out against pale sand. Short, dense spikes bloom in mid-spring, among the earliest penstemons to flower on the plains. It is well adapted to loose, sandy or gravelly soil with sharp drainage and minimal fertility, and resents heavy clay or excess moisture. Use it in a sand prairie restoration, dry rock garden, or gravel bed where its compact size and early bloom add interest before taller prairie perennials take over.

planting.note: Plant container-grown transplants in spring in lean, gravelly, extremely well-drained soil in full sun; this subalpine cliff-dweller needs sharp drainage and cool summers.

directions: Mountain penstemon forms a low, woody mat on rocky ledges, talus slopes, and limestone cliffs at subalpine elevations across the central and northern Rocky Mountains of Idaho, Utah, Wyoming, and Montana. In early summer it produces disproportionately large, vivid lavender-blue flowers against small, leathery, evergreen leaves. It is best grown in a trough, crevice garden, or raised rock bed with extremely sharp drainage and cool root conditions, and it struggles in hot, humid summer climates far from its alpine origins. Keep watering minimal once established and avoid any soil enrichment.

planting.note: Direct sow in fall or cold stratify before spring sowing in lean to average, well-drained soil in full sun; thrives on dry sandy or gravelly prairie ground.

directions: A slender, fine-textured native of dry prairies across the northern Great Plains and upper Midwest, lilac penstemon bears open spikes of pale lilac-pink to nearly white flowers with distinctive fine purple nectar-guide lines in early summer. Its slight build and narrow leaves let it weave unobtrusively among grasses and other prairie wildflowers rather than standing out as a bold specimen. Grow in lean, sandy or gravelly, well-drained soil in full sun; it is well suited to a prairie restoration or dry meadow planting and needs little attention once established.

planting.note: Direct sow in fall or cold stratify before spring sowing in average, well-drained soil in full sun; native to moist montane meadows so tolerates more regular water than desert penstemons.

directions: Rydberg's penstemon grows in erect clumps topped with tight, ball-like whorls of blue-purple tubular flowers stacked along the upper stem, blooming through summer in subalpine and montane meadows of the Rocky Mountains from Montana south to Arizona and New Mexico. Unlike many of its dryland relatives, it is native to seasonally moist mountain meadows and appreciates more regular moisture through the growing season, especially at planting. Grow in full sun in average garden soil with good drainage, and use it in a native meadow or moist rock garden setting where its tidy, upright form and long bloom period are an asset.

planting.note: Plant container-grown transplants in spring in lean, well-drained soil in full sun; needs sharp drainage and is drought tolerant once established.

directions: Scarlet bugler is one of the few true red-flowered penstemons, sending up tall, slender spikes lined with narrow, tubular, bright red-orange flowers through late spring and early summer. Native to dry chaparral, foothill grassland, and disturbed slopes across California and into Baja California, it has smooth, blue-gray, clasping leaves and a lanky, wand-like habit. Its narrow tubular flowers are shaped specifically for hummingbird pollination and make it an outstanding addition to a hummingbird or California native garden. Grow in lean, well-drained soil in full sun with little summer water; it tends to be short-lived but often self-sows where happy.

planting.note: Direct sow in fall or cold stratify before spring sowing in average, well-drained soil in full sun; tolerates garden conditions better than many dryland penstemons.

directions: Named for the Wasatch Range of Utah where it is especially abundant, this penstemon produces dense, upright spikes of vivid deep blue flowers in early summer above broad, somewhat glossy basal leaves, native to montane meadows and sagebrush slopes across the central Rocky Mountains. It is a sturdy, relatively easygoing species that adapts reasonably well to average garden soil, provided drainage is adequate, making it a good entry point for gardeners new to native penstemons. Grow in full sun with moderate water during establishment, then reduce watering; deadheading spent spikes can encourage a secondary flush of bloom.

planting.note: Plant container-grown transplants in spring in lean, gravelly, well-drained soil in full sun; a mat-forming high-elevation species needing sharp drainage.

directions: Mountain pride forms a dense, trailing mat of small, scalloped, gray-green evergreen leaves that lights up in early summer with a profusion of vivid rose-pink to magenta flowers, native to rocky slopes, ledges, and talus of the Sierra Nevada and southern Cascades. Its cascading habit and brilliant color make it a favorite for draping over a rock wall, scree slope, or raised bed edge. Plant in gritty, fast-draining soil in full sun and water sparingly once established; this high-elevation native performs best in cooler summer climates and can struggle with prolonged heat and humidity.

planting.note: Plant container-grown transplants in spring in lean, gravelly or clay-limestone soil in full sun; forms a very low, tight mat and needs sharp drainage.

directions: True to its name, mat penstemon forms an exceptionally low, dense, woody groundcover only an inch or two tall, native to dry rocky slopes and clay-limestone outcrops of the central Rocky Mountains in Utah, Colorado, and Wyoming. Small lavender-blue flowers stud the mat just above the tiny gray-green leaves in late spring. Its ground-hugging scale makes it ideal for tucking between flagstones, along a gravel path edge, or as a living mulch in a rock garden where taller plants would overwhelm it. Grow in lean, sharply drained soil in full sun and avoid any foot traffic or overwatering.

planting.note: Plant container-grown transplants in spring in lean, rocky, well-drained soil in full sun; a low woody subshrub of pinyon-juniper and dry Southwestern slopes.

directions: Toadflax penstemon is a low, spreading, woody-based subshrub with narrow, needle-like gray-green leaves that resemble those of toadflax, native to pinyon-juniper woodlands and dry rocky slopes across the Four Corners region of Arizona, New Mexico, Colorado, and Utah. Short spikes of blue-violet flowers appear in late spring to early summer, covering the small-scaled foliage. It is extremely drought tolerant once established and well suited to a xeriscape rock garden, dry slope, or gravel bed in a hot, sunny spot. Avoid rich soil, heavy mulch, or regular irrigation, which quickly rot its shallow woody roots.

planting.note: Plant divisions or container-grown transplants in spring in average, well-drained soil in full sun; this compact garden hybrid flowers over a long season with light deadheading.

directions: 'Evelyn' is a compact, long-blooming garden hybrid penstemon with narrow, fine-textured leaves and slender spikes of small, soft pink, tubular flowers produced in great abundance from early summer well into fall. Long popular in British perennial borders for its tidy habit and remarkably extended flowering window, it is less drought-tolerant than many wild species penstemons and performs best with average garden moisture and fertile, well-drained soil. Deadhead spent spikes regularly to keep flowers coming, and cut back old growth in late winter before new shoots emerge. It is somewhat less cold hardy than many North American native species.
